beats.lead: The story gets told as 'one man's veto stopped World War Three.'
beats.text: The stranger, truer version: that veto only existed on his boat because of where he happened to be standing.
beats.note: The other submarines in the same group didn't need his agreement at all.

beats.name: Soviet submarine B-59
beats.role: Cornered by US Navy destroyers off Cuba, out of radio contact with Moscow for days, carrying a nuclear torpedo with roughly the power of the Hiroshima bomb.

beats.lead: The US ships were only trying to force it to the surface.
beats.text: They dropped practice depth charges as a signal, not to sink it.
beats.note: Nobody aboard B-59 knew that. They didn't know if the war outside had already started.

beats.lead: Firing needed all three of the boat's senior officers to agree.
beats.text: Two said yes. The third was Vasily Arkhipov, the flotilla's chief of staff, who happened to be riding that particular submarine.
beats.note: On the other three boats in the group, only two signatures were needed — his rank was the only reason B-59 required three.

beats.context: How long the story stayed buried — first acknowledged at a 1997 Moscow conference, fully confirmed at a 2002 Havana conference where both sides compared notes for the first time.

beats.line: The vote that only existed because of who happened to be on board.
